# Results — Study 437 (Donchian-Breakout) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The 20-day Donchian
channel breakout, stripped of the rest of the Turtle apparatus: **go long when the
close makes a new 20-day high; go flat when it makes a new 20-day low** (long/flat).
Costs charged one-way × NAV at every switch (2 bps); one documented execution lag
(channel uses bars up to t-1, position entered at t+1). Raced NET, on the same flat-cash
baseline, against buy-and-hold, an SMA(20) cross benchmark, and a matched random-timing
control. Tested on SPY daily total-return closes (`auto_adjust=True`) from 1993-01-29 to
2026-06-12 (n = 8,400 days). As-of **2026-06-23**.*

## Data stamp

| Ticker | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPY | 1993-01-29 → 2026-06-12 | 8,400 | `bc9ada8a0d6f` |

Panel (generality probe): QQQ `367fef3aa630` (n=6,858), IWM `8e20d3c81843` (n=2,515),
TLT `7a1b06cf3a49` (n=6,007), GLD `87fdeb0317e4` (n=5,425), USO `0f1664cccc70` (n=5,076),
UUP `63ef64d704b5` (n=4,853).

## The four arms — Donchian-20 vs buy-and-hold vs SMA(20) vs random (SPY, net 2 bps)

A long/flat rule sits in cash part of the time, so the fair race is excess-vs-excess of
the same flat baseline (cash = 0%). The random-timing control matches the breakout rule's
in-market fraction (62.2%) on random days, isolating *timing skill* from exposure.

| Arm | CAGR | Sharpe | Vol | Max drawdown | HAC *t* (own mean) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Buy-and-hold** | **+10.82%** | **+0.553** | 18.6% | **−55.2%** | +3.67 |
| **Donchian-20 long/flat** | +5.16% | +0.465 | 10.8% | −41.9% | +2.90 |
| SMA(20) cross | +3.68% | +0.325 | 11.1% | −44.3% | +1.94 |
| Random timing (null) | +3.72% | +0.258 | 14.2% | −70.1% | +1.57 |

- **Donchian vs buy-and-hold:** HAC *t* on the daily return *difference* = **−2.32** —
  the breakout rule's risk-adjusted return is *significantly worse* than just holding SPY.
  Its lower Sharpe (+0.465 < +0.553) is not noise; you lose, net, by timing.
- **Donchian's own *t* = +2.90 is beta, not breakout skill.** The rule is long 62% of the
  time in a market that rises — of course the in-sample mean is positive. The inference
  bar is the edge *versus the benchmark*, and that edge is negative.
- **Donchian vs random timing:** HAC *t* = **+0.66** — not distinguishable. The breakout
  picks days only marginally better than a coin with the same exposure.
- **Donchian vs SMA(20):** HAC *t* = **+0.94** — **not significant**. "The channel is
  better than a plain moving average" is *not supported*: the two are statistically tied,
  and both lose to buy-and-hold.
- **In-market fraction:** 62.2%; 203 switches over 33 years (~6/year).

## The block-permutation placebo — does the *timing* carry information?

Shuffle the position schedule in 20-day blocks (preserving the clustering of being
positioned, destroying its alignment with the return tape) and re-run, gross:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| Real rule mean (gross) | **+2.05 bps/day** |
| Permutation *p*-value (2,000 perms, block = 20) | **0.83** |

A *p* of 0.83 means **83% of random in/out schedules with the same exposure beat the real
Donchian schedule**. The breakout's days-in-market are, if anything, slightly *worse* than
random ones — there is no timing information in the channel.

## Cost sensitivity (SPY, net Sharpe)

Low turnover (~6 switches/yr), so costs are not what kills it — the rule is simply behind
buy-and-hold at every cost level:

| One-way cost | Sharpe | CAGR | *t* vs BH |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | +0.477 | +5.29% | −2.27 |
| 1 bps | +0.471 | +5.23% | −2.29 |
| 2 bps | +0.465 | +5.16% | −2.32 |
| 5 bps | +0.449 | +4.97% | −2.40 |
| 10 bps | +0.420 | +4.65% | −2.53 |

## Window robustness (SPY long/flat, net 2 bps)

The classic N = 20 is the *worst-looking* short window; only the very slow channels close
the Sharpe gap to buy-and-hold — and none of them clear it:

| N | Donchian Sharpe | BH Sharpe | *t* vs BH |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 10 | +0.331 | +0.553 | −3.03 |
| 20 | +0.465 | +0.553 | −2.32 |
| 55 | +0.523 | +0.553 | −1.89 |
| 100 | +0.603 | +0.553 | −1.44 |

The slowest channel (N=100) finally nudges past BH in raw Sharpe but the difference is not
significant (*t* = −1.44 in BH's favour, i.e. still not a win) — and a 100-day channel is
no longer the "20-day breakout" of the folklore.

## Long/short variant (SPY, net 2 bps, 50 bps/yr borrow)

Adding the short leg (go short on new 20-day lows) destroys the rule outright — equities
trend up, so the short side bleeds:

| Metric | Value |
|---|--:|
| Sharpe | −0.015 |
| CAGR | −0.27% |
| Max drawdown | −62.9% |
| *t* vs BH | −2.34 |

## Panel — does it generalise?

Donchian-20 long/flat fails to beat buy-and-hold on every liquid equity/bond/metal tape;
the one positive head-to-head (USO crude, *t* = +1.57) is not significant and rides a
secularly *falling* asset where any de-risking rule looks good:

| Ticker | n | Donchian Sharpe | BH Sharpe | *t* vs BH |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 8,399 | +0.465 | +0.553 | −2.32 |
| QQQ | 6,857 | +0.349 | +0.385 | −1.32 |
| IWM | 2,514 | +0.498 | +0.461 | −0.53 |
| TLT | 6,006 | +0.217 | +0.255 | −0.75 |
| GLD | 5,424 | +0.324 | +0.553 | −2.29 |
| USO | 5,075 | +0.183 | −0.195 | +1.57 |
| UUP | 4,852 | −0.069 | +0.197 | −1.59 |

## Synthetic control — the engine *can* bank a real breakout edge

A deterministic AR(1) tape with a **planted-edge knob** (``edge`` = return
autocorrelation): at ``edge = 0`` (a random walk) the breakout must add nothing; at
``edge = 0.4`` (strong trend persistence) it must light up. The harness passes both:

| Tape | Donchian Sharpe | BH Sharpe | *t* vs BH | Permutation *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Null (edge = 0) | −0.414 | −0.295 | +0.11 | 0.92 |
| Trend (edge = 0.4) | +0.052 | −0.446 | **+2.24** | **0.044** |

On the planted-trend tape the breakout beats buy-and-hold at *t* = +2.24 and the placebo
lights up (*p* = 0.044). The engine is faithful: it *would* certify a real channel edge if
one existed on SPY. It doesn't — so the null result is the engine working, not failing.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The 20-day Donchian breakout's *timing* carries no information on
  SPY: the block-permutation placebo *p* = 0.83 (random schedules beat it 83% of the time),
  it loses to buy-and-hold on a risk-adjusted basis at HAC *t* = −2.32, and it is
  statistically tied with a plain SMA(20) (*t* = +0.94) and with a matched random control
  (*t* = +0.66). The rule's own +2.90 *t* is bull-market beta from being long 62% of the
  time, not breakout skill — and the inference bar is the edge *versus the benchmark*,
  which is negative. The synthetic positive control (*t* = +2.24, placebo *p* = 0.044 with
  a planted trend) proves the harness *can* detect a channel edge; SPY simply has none.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Even gross, the rule trails buy-and-hold (Sharpe +0.477 vs
  +0.553); net of trivial costs it is further behind; the long/short variant goes negative
  (Sharpe −0.015); it fails across the whole panel. The only thing it reliably delivers is
  *lower drawdown* (−42% vs −55%) — but that is just lower equity exposure (62% invested),
  and you can buy the same drawdown reduction far more cheaply with a 60/40 split, no timing
  required.
- **"Better than a plain SMA"? — NOT SUPPORTED.** Same window, same lag, same costs: the
  Donchian channel and the SMA(20) cross are statistically indistinguishable (*t* = +0.94),
  and both lose to buy-and-hold. The channel's extra machinery (a state that carries between
  breaks) buys nothing measurable over the simplest moving-average filter.
